claims.text: The high-entropy alloy is a near-equiatomic mixture of transition metals with significant atomic-scale compositional disorder.
A low-entropy alloy containing fewer elements can retain similar overall stoichiometry while having reduced configurational disorder.
Randomly distributed atomic species cause local lattice distortions.
Compositional disorder produces variable bond lengths.
Variable bond lengths and local lattice distortions enhance electron-phonon coupling.
Enhanced electron-phonon coupling strengthens the superconducting pairing interaction.
Stronger superconducting pairing caused by enhanced electron-phonon coupling can raise the superconducting critical temperature.
The high-entropy alloy will have a higher superconducting critical temperature than the low-entropy baseline.
The high-entropy alloy will have a larger superconducting energy gap than the low-entropy baseline.
The high-entropy alloy will show stronger indicators of electron-phonon coupling than the low-entropy baseline.
Using identical synthesis and test conditions makes configurational disorder the primary source of any observed superconducting differences.
Disorder-induced lattice distortions are expected to dominate superconducting behavior when they are significant in multicomponent alloys.
The proposed electron-phonon mechanism may not govern superconductivity when magnetic fluctuations or strong electron correlations are the primary pairing drivers.
